overview: Brachiosaurus was a high-shouldered sauropod from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of North America. Its front legs were longer than its hind legs, giving it a distinctive giraffe-like outline.

NHM lists it at around 22 metres long and 46.9 tonnes. The local DK guide uses slightly rounder figures and describes the animal as a Jurassic high browser, while noting features such as chisel-shaped teeth and nostrils set high on the skull.

articles.title: High browsing body plan
articles.body: Brachiosaurus had a deep chest, long neck and raised shoulders. This made it very different in outline from low-slung diplodocids such as Diplodocus and Apatosaurus.

articles.title: Feeding and teeth
articles.body: NHM describes it as eating leaves from tall trees and swallowing plant matter without chewing. DK notes chisel-shaped teeth, which fit stripping vegetation rather than grinding it in the mouth.

articles.title: Posture and reconstruction
articles.body: The broad idea of high browsing is secure, but exact neck posture is still interpreted cautiously. NHM also notes that some full-body reconstructions have relied heavily on the related African Giraffatitan.

articles.title: Morrison habitat
articles.body: Brachiosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic Morrison ecosystem with stegosaurs, diplodocids and large theropods. Its size and browsing height let it use a different feeding zone from many neighbours.

fossilRecord.material: Partial skeleton of Brachiosaurus altithorax; many older reconstructions also use comparison with Giraffatitan.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Jurassic Morrison ecosystem, probably browsing at different heights from many diplodocids.
fossilRecord.evidence: Elevated shoulder anatomy and distinctive limb proportions distinguish it from low-slung diplodocids.

record.description: Brachiosaurus altithorax was a brachiosaurid sauropod from the Morrison Formation of Colorado. Its holotype is a partial postcranial skeleton; the well-known African skeletons once called Brachiosaurus brancai belong to the separate genus Giraffatitan.
facts: The holotype FMNH P 25107 was found by Elmer Riggs's team in 1900 near Fruita, Colorado, and described in 1903; it comprises dorsal and sacral vertebrae, ribs, a coracoid, humerus, ilium and femur.
No skull is confidently associated with B. altithorax; a Morrison skull (USNM 5730) once assigned to Camarasaurus may belong to Brachiosaurus but is not from the holotype.
Long forelimbs and a high shoulder are supported by the holotype, while many popular details derive from Giraffatitan and must not be transferred uncritically.
Taylor's 2009 re-evaluation formalised the separation of the Tanzanian material as Giraffatitan brancai.
Referred Morrison material is limited and some referrals are debated.

presentation.heroLead: The high-shouldered giant of the Morrison Formation, known from one partial skeleton that anchors a name long applied, wrongly, to more complete African relatives.

animalParagraphs: Brachiosaurus was one of the largest animals of the Late Jurassic, a sauropod with forelimbs longer than its hindlimbs, a steeply sloping back and a neck that could be raised well above the shoulders. The holotype suggests an animal around twenty metres long and several tens of tonnes in weight.

It lived on the seasonally dry floodplains of the Morrison Formation alongside Apatosaurus, Diplodocus and Camarasaurus, and probably browsed higher in the canopy than those flatter-backed neighbours. Its teeth were spoon-shaped and its nostrils sat high on the skull, if the referred skull is correctly assigned.

Much of what the public knows as Brachiosaurus, including the famous mounted skeleton in Berlin, is actually Giraffatitan from Tanzania. The North American animal itself is known from a single partial skeleton and a handful of other bones, so its proportions are less secure than its fame suggests.
animalHighlights: Forelimbs longer than the hindlimbs, giving a high shoulder and a back that sloped down to the hips.
A deep, broad ribcage indicated by the holotype's dorsal vertebrae; the species name means "deep chest".
One of the heaviest Morrison dinosaurs, although no complete individual allows a precise mass.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Long forelimbs and neck suggest feeding in tree canopies; the spoon-shaped teeth are known from the referred skull and from Giraffatitan.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: The humerus and femur of the holotype establish its columnar, four-legged stance and unusual limb proportions.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Length and mass are scaled from the holotype using proportions borrowed from Giraffatitan; estimates span 30 to 60 tonnes.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: No skull is certainly associated and the neck is not preserved in the holotype; both follow related genera.

presentation.classificationSummary: Brachiosaurus is the name-bearing genus of Brachiosauridae within Titanosauriformes. Giraffatitan, once treated as a species of Brachiosaurus, is now a separate genus; other brachiosaurids include Lusotitan from Portugal and Sonorasaurus from Arizona.

related.reason: The far more complete Tanzanian relative long confused with it.
A common Morrison macronarian with a similar skull type.
A contemporary sauropod with the opposite body plan: low shoulders and a whip tail.

questions.title: What did its skull look like?
questions.copy: A Morrison skull once assigned to Camarasaurus is probably brachiosaurid and may be Brachiosaurus, but it is not associated with the holotype.

questions.title: How big was it really?
questions.copy: With only one partial skeleton, length and mass depend on assumptions borrowed from Giraffatitan. Estimates range widely.

questions.title: How much referred material is Brachiosaurus?
questions.copy: Several Morrison specimens have been referred to the genus on limb proportions alone; some of these referrals are questioned.

review.ageReviewNote: The holotype is Kimmeridgian within the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation.

evidence.summary: One principal partial postcranial skeleton establishes the distinctive body plan, but the skull, neck and most of the limbs are unknown or referred, and the famous complete skeletons belong to Giraffatitan.
evidence.material: Holotype FMNH P 25107: seven dorsal vertebrae, sacrum, two caudal vertebrae, ribs, right coracoid, right humerus, right ilium and right femur; plus limited referred Morrison material.
formations: Morrison Formation, Brushy Basin Member — Colorado and Utah, USA
evidence.confidenceLimit: The basic postcranial build is supported; skull, neck completeness, maximum size and species variation are poorly constrained.
evidence.sourceBasis: Riggs 1903/1904, Taylor 2009/2011 and the Natural History Museum synthesis.

panel.headline: One partial skeleton from Colorado carries the whole genus.
panel.standfirst: Brachiosaurus altithorax rests on a single partial postcranial skeleton excavated in 1900. Its unusual limb proportions are directly preserved, but the skull, neck and most of the rest of the animal are known only from referred bones or from the separate genus Giraffatitan.

coverage.label: Moderate
coverage.basis: Trunk vertebrae, sacrum, one humerus, one femur and girdle elements are preserved; the skull, neck, tail and most limb bones are missing from the holotype.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The holotype preserves seven dorsal vertebrae, the sacrum, two caudal vertebrae, ribs, the right coracoid, right humerus, right ilium and right femur. Referred material adds a possible skull, isolated vertebrae and limb bones from other Morrison sites.
knownRemains.note: Riggs excavated the skeleton from a hillside near Fruita; erosion had already removed the front and much of the rear of the animal before discovery.

materialGroups.value: None with the holotype. USNM 5730 from Garden Park is a brachiosaurid skull that may belong to the genus.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Seven dorsal vertebrae, the sacrum and two caudal vertebrae in the holotype; no cervical vertebrae.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: None. No skin, colour or gut contents are known.

specimenCards.title: FMNH P 25107 · holotype
specimenCards.description: Found by H. W. Menke of Elmer Riggs's Field Columbian Museum expedition in 1900 on a hill near Fruita, Colorado, and described by Riggs in 1903 as the largest known dinosaur. The humerus alone is over two metres long.
specimenCards.meta: Riggs Hill, Mesa County, Colorado · Morrison Formation · Field Museum of Natural History

specimenCards.title: Giraffatitan brancai
specimenCards.description: The mounted skeletons from Tendaguru, Tanzania, were described as Brachiosaurus brancai in 1914 and long defined the public image of the genus. Since 2009 they are treated as the separate genus Giraffatitan and must not be used to fill gaps in B. altithorax.
specimenCards.meta: Tendaguru Formation · Museum für Naturkunde, Berlin

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Deep dorsal vertebrae, a sacrum, a long humerus and a femur from one individual, establishing the high-shouldered sauropod body plan.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A very large brachiosaurid high browser, distinct from its African relative in vertebral and limb proportions.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: The skull and neck, the tail, precise size and mass, and how many Morrison bones truly belong to the genus.
